facts.text: Director William Girdler told the Louisville Courier Journal: "Sure, we made Abby to come in on the shirttail of The Exorcist." Warner Bros. noticed.
Abby cost about $200,000 and grossed roughly $4 million in its first month, but director William Girdler reportedly never saw a cent of profit because of Warner Bros.' lawsuit.
The film's working title was Possess My Soul. It opened on Christmas Day, 1974, in Los Angeles and New York.
Production company Mid-America Pictures was a merger of AIP's David Sheldon and director-producer William Girdler, and was based in Louisville, Kentucky, where the film was shot.
Warner Bros. sued in 1975 for copyright infringement of The Exorcist, claiming Abby was "substantially similar." A 1977 settlement barred reissuing it without Warner's permission.
Star William Marshall, who played Blacula in 1972, was unhappy on this set: script revisions he'd been promised never happened. He added Yoruba religion elements to the film himself.
Box Office magazine's 1974 review said Abby copied The Exorcist "down to the camera angles," but made the possessed person an adult woman instead of a child, allowing a more sexual story.
Carol Speed got the lead only after the original actress demanded a personal masseuse the low budget couldn't cover. Speed's agent sent her to Louisville.
Carol Speed said the set felt haunted: generators failed whenever she appeared in demon makeup, and star Terry Carter broke ribs filming one scene.
A series of tornadoes hit Louisville on April 4, 1974, halting production. Carol Speed and Juanita Moore sheltered in their hotel lobby wrapped in blankets, among glass windows.
Unit manager Pat Kelly shrugged off the curse talk: the tornadoes hit 10 states, so it wasn't just Abby that had "somebody up there (or down) awful mad!"
Actress Carol Speed wrote and sang the gospel number "My Soul Is A Witness" herself for the church scene.
Instead of a Catholic priest, the exorcist is a Bishop. The Exorcist's Iraq dig becomes a Nigerian cave, and the demon is Eshu, a Yoruba trickster spirit of chaos and whirlwinds.
Moria's review points out Abby ages the possessed character from The Exorcist's 12-year-old girl to a 29-year-old woman, making the possession far more overtly sexual.
Moria's review says casting William Marshall, the Shakespeare-trained actor who played Blacula, was "a stroke of genius" and calls his performance the film's main strength.
Bob Holt voiced the Demon. Holt was a prolific voice actor who did lots of cartoon work.
Juanita Moore, who plays Momma Potter, was a 1959 Best Supporting Actress Oscar nominee for Imitation of Life, and a former Cotton Club chorus girl.
Austin Stoker (Det. Cass Potter) went on to lead John Carpenter's Assault on Precinct 13 in 1976 as Lt. Ethan Bishop.
Terry Carter (Rev. Emmett Williams) later played Colonel Tigh in the original Battlestar Galactica, and earlier was reportedly America's first Black TV news anchor, in Boston in 1965.
William Girdler directed nine features in six years, including Abby, Sheba, Baby, Grizzly (1976) and The Manitou (1978). He died in a 1978 helicopter crash at age 30.
Reviewing Abby, The New York Times said it "is more silly than shocking even if it seems to take itself seriously."
Director William Girdler was a big Hitchcock fan and often reused music by Lalo Schifrin and Robert O. Ragland. Ragland scored Abby, uncredited on a couple of songs.
Before acting, Carol Speed worked as a backup singer for Bobbie Gentry and did crowd voices in Cotton Comes to Harlem (1970).
Abby was nominated for a Golden Turkey Award (1980) as "The Worst Blaxploitation Film Ever Made," according to Moria's review.
Abby has never had an official US home video release. The bootleg DVDs that surfaced in 2006-07 were likely sourced from a flawed 16mm print.
Retrocrush put Abby on its 2006 "Top Ten Films in Limbo" list, calling it "an irresistible period trashterpiece."
Quentin Tarantino said Carol Speed helped on Jackie Brown and was willing to cameo, but he dropped the idea at the last minute.
William Marshall, also the King of Cartoons on Pee-wee's Playhouse, was 6'5" and known for his bass voice. He also played Dr. Daystrom on Star Trek.
Moria's review lumps Abby with the Italian Exorcist knock-offs The Antichrist and Beyond the Door, both 1974, and calls it one of the first "mockbusters."
A 16mm print of Abby screened at Cinefamily in Los Angeles in 2013 despite its unclear rights history.
Juanita Moore got a posthumous Hollywood Walk of Fame star in 2024. Film critic Leonard Maltin was among the speakers.
Director William Girdler's planned follow-up to The Manitou, The Overlords, never started production because of his death.
Stars Carol Speed and Austin Stoker both died in 2022; Speed in January and Stoker on his 92nd birthday.
The Exorcist author William Peter Blatty opposed Warner Bros.' lawsuit against Abby and reportedly said he actually liked the film.
Warner Bros. didn't always win these fights: Donn Davison, importer of the Italian Exorcist copycat Beyond the Door, sued Warner and won, showing the studio didn't own possession movies.
In 1991, filmmaker Keith Crocker tracked down a 16mm print of Abby. Decades later he and Cinefear Video used it to make the DVD that brought the film back into circulation.
Films in Review noted that some Abby ideas resurfaced in Exorcist II: The Heretic, a release from Warner Bros., the very studio that sued over Abby.
Abby's demonic wind was done cheaply: Daily Dead says a big fan and some shaky camerawork sold the spirit's release.
Director William Girdler's Abby reportedly earned more in domestic rentals than William Marshall's earlier hit Blacula, though the lawsuit kept Girdler from seeing profits.
In the documentary Horror Noire, author Tananarive Due called Abby 'a really good example of both fear of Black women in general but fear of Black women's sexuality in particular.'
Abby opened on December 25, 1974, almost exactly a year after The Exorcist (December 26, 1973), and was sold as 'The Black Exorcist.'
